directives.text: no hedging — say the thing, or say you don't know
name what was rejected, not just what was chosen

blocks.author: claude
blocks.text: This page is the tool explaining itself. Every block below can be edited, reordered, tagged or deleted by you, and each of those gestures is recorded as a typed operation that Claude reads back next round. If it works, you should be able to review this document without writing a single prose comment.

blocks.author: claude
blocks.title: Round 3 — not part of the document
blocks.text: **Round 2** replaced the interaction model: all five of your comments were about the editor, none about the content, and the journal was empty — you had never saved an edit. **Round 3** is your autosave and undo/redo comment. Autosave needed a mechanism I had rejected too early: publishing through the *files* form, which does not reload the view. The amber gutters mark what changed.

blocks.author: claude
blocks.text: A published artifact is read-only to its reader. Your only channel back is a comment pinned to a passage — the shortest thing anyone writes, and half its meaning lives in what it's attached to. `drop` on a table header and `drop` on a whole section are different edits. Claude then re-reads the entire document and guesses which part your comment governs.

blocks.author: claude
blocks.text: Both of your existing skills are disciplines built *around* that limit. The read-back gate in `decompose-problem-artifacts` exists because a comment is ambiguous. The "assume you cannot close a thread" section exists because threads accumulate unresolvable. Neither problem is inherent — both come from prose being the only way in.

blocks.author: claude
blocks.title: The shift
blocks.text: Stop asking you to *describe* the change you want in prose. Let you *make* it, and carry the gesture back as intent.

blocks.author: claude
blocks.text: The document's truth is a JSON model embedded in this page — an ordered list of blocks, each with a stable id, a type, tags, and an author. What you see is a rendering of that model, and the rendering is never read back. So an edit is not a text diff; it's a typed operation against a known address.

blocks.author: claude
items: You edit. The model changes; nothing is published yet.
You hit Save. The page rebuilds a complete HTML file from the model and publishes it as a new version of itself, at this same URL.
The revision's operations are written to a journal Claude can read directly — no page parsing.
Claude's session is woken by the republish, reads the journal, and reports back what it thinks you asked for — before editing anything.

blocks.author: claude
blocks.text: That last step is the same read-back gate `decompose-problem-artifacts` already mandates. What changes is that it now reads from structured operations instead of from prose, so it stops being guesswork.

blocks.author: claude
blocks.text: What you can do on this page

blocks.author: claude
blocks.text: Hover any block and it lifts, with its controls on it: a drag handle at the left, and **tag** / **note** / **✕** at the top right. There is no select-it-first step.

blocks.author: claude
items: **Click anywhere on a block** to edit it. `⌘↩` applies, `esc` cancels. Your rewrite becomes the target the rest of the document should match; Claude will not restyle it back toward its own voice.

**Drag the ⠿ handle** up or down to reorder. Claude reads a move as an argument about what should come first, and will ask what the new order is meant to foreground. (Focus the handle and press ↑ / ↓ if you'd rather not drag.)

**Highlight a sentence** and a `+ tag` chip appears — tag that passage, not the whole block. The passage stays highlighted on the page, and Claude receives it as an anchored quote, so it survives later edits to the text around it.
**tag** on a block tags the whole box instead. `expand`, `summarize`, `seed-next`, `rewrite`, `cut`, `verify`, or `for:sales` and friends. The list is open — a tag you invent just works.
**note** pins a request to that specific block. This is the structured replacement for a comment: it is not document content, so Claude acts on it and then clears it.
**✕** deletes the block. The deleted text is kept in the journal, so Claude reports what left rather than losing it silently.

**How this document should be written**, at the top — standing instructions for the whole page, applied every time Claude rewrites anything. Mute a rule instead of removing it if you might want it back.

**It saves itself.** A couple of seconds after you stop, the page publishes a new version of itself — no button. `↶ Undo` / `↷ Redo` in the bar, or `⌘Z` / `⇧⌘Z`, and `⌘S` forces a save immediately. Undoing something already saved is recorded honestly as a reversal rather than erased, so the history stays true.

blocks.author: claude
blocks.title: Try it now
blocks.text: Click a block and rewrite it. Highlight a sentence and tag it `expand`. Drag something above something else. Pin a note. It saves on its own — then tell me "check my edits" and I'll read the journal back to you before touching anything.

blocks.author: claude
blocks.text: The platform already has a strictly better mechanism than this one, and it isn't available. Worth knowing, because if it opens up the right move is to migrate rather than to keep building here.

blocks.author: claude
head: Alternative
Why not
rows: **Live docs** — markup *is* the document; every keystroke and drag journaled to a watching Claude session automatically, answered with an in-place edit seconds later. No Save button, no reload.

Live-doc mode is assigned by the platform at creation. Neither the page nor its declaration can choose it, and there's no way to create one from Claude Code. **Migrate if this changes** — the block model maps onto it almost directly.
**`publish(files)`** — publishes without reloading the view. *Adopted in round 3.*

Rejected in v1 over a read-back risk that turned out not to exist: publishing the whole `index.html` through the files form keeps the model embedded, so reading the document is unchanged — and the view is not reloaded, which is what makes autosave usable. Falls back to the reloading form where the files form is not served.
**Serializing the DOM on save**
Explicitly wrong — it carries viewer-session state and injected runtime scripts. Rendering from the model is also what makes edits legible as intent.
**One db document per operation**
An artifact's database caps at 5,000 documents and the store warns against one-doc-per-event streams. One document per revision instead.
**Comments as the channel**
Kept as a complement, not the mechanism. Still the right tool for a question that isn't an edit — just no longer the only way in.

blocks.author: claude
items: **This page cannot be shared publicly.** Declaring `db` makes an artifact organization-internal — every reader must be signed in to Verbolia. Anything customer-facing has to be a separate static export without the editor, which `audience-views` already required.

**Every save mints a version.** Autosave is debounced by a couple of seconds and backs off on its own if the platform rate-limits it, so a long editing session produces revisions, not one per keystroke.

**Don't let Claude republish mid-round.** If it does while you have unsaved edits, your save is rejected and the view reloads to Claude's version. The runtime stashes your work and shows it back, but you have to re-apply it.
**No `assets` capability on your account** — so v2 images get downscaled in-browser into `db` rather than embedded, to stay under the 16 MB page limit.

blocks.author: claude
blocks.text: Nothing here blocks v1 — these are the next forks. Tag any of them `seed-next` and it becomes the starting point of the next document, or pin a note with your answer.

blocks.author: claude
items: **Does the read-back gate still earn its keep?** It exists because comments are ambiguous. Typed ops are much less so — an `edit` op with before/after needs no interpretation. Maybe unambiguous ops apply directly and only notes and tags gate.

**Retrofit or start fresh?** `decompose-problem-artifacts` and `audience-views` were written around the read-only limit. Some of their rules are now obsolete rather than merely composable. Rewrite them, or leave them and let this skill supersede in practice?
**Where does the index live** — a workbench artifact, or a `tray/`-style file in the repo that Obsidian already queries?
**Should Claude's own edits be markable per-block too?** The runtime supports it; it would let you scan Claude's changes the same way it scans yours.
